summary.7-10: A shepherd boy beats a giant.
summary.11-14: The smallest person in the army wins the fight.
summary.15-18: A theological argument disguised as a duel.

7-10: A giant called Goliath came out every day and shouted at God's people. Everybody was too scared to fight him.
David was just a boy looking after sheep. He said, “I will go.” The king gave him armour, but it was far too big, so David took it off.
He picked up five smooth stones from a stream, put one in his sling, and knocked the giant down. God had helped him.
11-14: For forty days a Philistine champion, over nine feet tall in armour nobody else could carry, came out and dared Israel to send someone against him. Nobody moved.
David arrived with food for his brothers, heard Goliath, and asked the question nobody else was asking: who is this man that he can insult the living God? His oldest brother told him to go home.

Saul offered him armour. David tried it, found he could not walk, and took it off. He went out with a stick, a sling and five stones from the stream, and said out loud that the battle belonged to God. Then he ran towards the giant.
15-18: The story is told as a contest of size and equipment, and everything in it is measured — Goliath's height, the weight of his coat of mail, the weight of his spearhead. The narrator wants you counting.

Against all that, David's refusal of Saul's armour is the decisive act. He rejects the terms of the contest as everyone else has defined them, and states the alternative plainly: 'the battle is the Lord's'.

It is also worth noticing what a sling was. In ancient armies slingers were a genuine unit, capable of lethal accuracy at a distance. The story is not that a helpless child got lucky; it is that Israel's fear had made them measure the wrong things, and one shepherd measured them against God instead.

whatHappened.7-10: David trusted God and beat a giant that everyone else was afraid of.
whatHappened.11-14: David faced the champion nobody else would face, refused the king's armour, and won with a sling and God's help.
whatHappened.15-18: David reframes an impossible military problem as a theological one, and acts on that reframing.

whatItTeaches.7-10: You do not have to be big for God to use you.
whatItTeaches.11-14: The problem was never Goliath's size. It was that Israel was measuring the giant against themselves instead of against God.
whatItTeaches.15-18: The narrative's argument is about the frame, not the odds: what looks impossible depends entirely on what you measure it against.

thinkAboutIt.7-10: What is your Goliath at the moment — the thing that feels too big?
thinkAboutIt.11-14: David refused armour that did not fit him. Where are you trying to fight with someone else's equipment?
thinkAboutIt.15-18: Everyone in that valley had the same facts and drew a different conclusion. What are you currently measuring against the wrong thing?

pray.7-10: God, when things feel too big for me, help me remember you are bigger.
pray.11-14: God, help me face the thing I am avoiding, and to measure it against you rather than against myself.
pray.15-18: God, give me David's question rather than the army's fear — and the nerve to act on the answer.

prompt.7-10: What did David take with him to fight Goliath?
prompt.11-14: What did David take, and what did he leave behind?
prompt.15-18: What is the significance of David refusing Saul's armour?

explain.7-10: A sling and five smooth stones from the stream.
explain.11-14: A sling and five stones — and he left the king's armour behind because he could not move in it.
explain.15-18: Refusing the armour rejects the contest's assumed terms; David states the alternative outright: 'the battle is the Lord's'.
